title: Faith, four months in
excerpt: Four months back in church, a little awkwardness during worship, and a couple of questions about Psalm 138 and 2 Samuel 6.

body.alt: Jae’s cartoon character in his red jester hat, reading a Bible with blue hydrangeas beside him.

body.text: i have been going back to church for about four months-ish now. Honestly, it has been quite the journey, from attending Sunday services to joining ALPHA on Wednesdays and finishing the classes in October. i guess i am beginning to understand what people mean when they say faith is a journey. That being said, i still have a long way to go 🙂
This Sunday’s service focused on Psalm 138 and 2 Samuel 6. The main discussion was about praise and worship, and what it means to worship God.

Since i was young, i have always found it a little awkward to raise my hands during worship, ngl. The furthest i have gone is clasping my hands together or raising them somewhere around my midsection HAHA. So dancing or moving around during worship is definitely something i am not accustomed to.
i also had a couple of questions during the service, so naturally, i asked Kai, my trusty ChatGPT.
1) In Psalm 138:1, why is the word “gods” mentioned? Does it refer to the pagan gods people worshipped back then or something?
Kai’s answer:
That is one possible interpretation! Some understand “gods” here as the gods worshipped by surrounding nations, with the psalmist declaring his praise for God in their presence.

However, there is no single agreed interpretation. Other translations and commentators understand the word as referring to heavenly beings or angels, and some interpret it as rulers or judges. Across these readings, the emphasis is on wholehearted praise for God and his supremacy. The verse is not an invitation to worship other gods.
Further reading: translation commentary on Psalm 138:1
Commentary on Psalm 138
2) In 2 Samuel 6:13, David sacrifices animals. Was animal sacrifice common back then? Why did people do it, and why do we no longer practise it as Christians?
Kai’s answer:

Yes, animal sacrifice was an established part of worship in ancient Israel. Different offerings served different purposes, including thanksgiving, devotion, purification and atonement for sin. They were a way for people to honour God and express their relationship with him through something valuable to them. So sacrifices were not always about asking for forgiveness; they could also express gratitude and celebration.
In 2 Samuel 6, David offers sacrifices while bringing the Ark of the Covenant to Jerusalem. The chapter places these offerings alongside joyful worship, including David dancing before God.

As Christians, we do not offer animal sacrifices because we believe Jesus offered himself once for all. Hebrews 10 explains that his sacrifice accomplishes what repeated animal offerings could not, so further sacrifices for sin are unnecessary.

There is also a separate historical point: Jewish Temple sacrifices ended when the Romans destroyed the Second Temple in Jerusalem in AD 70. That is distinct from the Christian belief about Jesus; Jewish worship continued through prayer, study and other religious practices.

i know i need to be more proactive in this journey, and there is still plenty for me to learn and work on. i hope that, with time, i can grow into the person i aspire to be.
